content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2009 on the procurement and supply management of products for tuberculosis and malaria. These guidelines were accessed in February 2012. 2. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) released the 17th edition of its model regulations on the transport of dangerous goods in 2011. These recommendations were accessed in February 2012. 3. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations issued guidelines on good labeling practices for pesticides in 1995. These guidelines were accessed in February 2012. 4. The Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) provides a handbook and guidelines for pesticide analysis. These resources were accessed in February 2012. 5. CIPAC, FAO, and WHO jointly developed guidelines for the quality control of pesticide products, specifically for national laboratories. These guidelines were accessed in February 2012. 6. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) inspection manual in 2002. This document was accessed in February 2012. 7. The International Standards Organization (ISO) released standards on random sampling and randomization procedures in 2009 (ISO 24153). 8. WHO conducted a technical consultation in 2005 on the specifications and quality control of netting materials and mosquito nets. This document was accessed in February 2012. 9. ISO published standards in 2006 (ISO 2859-10) on sampling procedures for inspection by attributes, specifically introducing the ISO 2859 series. 10. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) released the 8th edition of its infectious substances shipping guidelines in 2007. 11. This document was accessed in February 2012. 12. Guidelines for procuring public health pesticides include detailed instructions for inviting tenders for pesticide supply. These guidelines specify the requirements for product descriptions, tender reference numbers, supply dates, and closing dates for submissions. Tenders must be submitted in sealed envelopes with the reference number clearly marked and delivered to the specified location before the deadline. Late submissions will not be accepted. 13. General conditions for tenders include the following: Tenderers must complete all required documents and price schedules. The procurement entity is not responsible for delays or losses of tender documents. Each product will be evaluated separately. Tenders must include sufficient data and evidence to demonstrate compliance with specifications. Prices must include costs for packaging, labeling, insurance, transport, and delivery. Contracts may not necessarily be awarded to the lowest bidder, as other factors such as quality, safety, and technical support are considered. Tenders must remain valid for the specified period after the opening date. Tenderers bear all costs associated with preparing and submitting their tenders. Representatives of tenderers may witness the opening of tenders. Tenderers must not contact the procurement entity regarding their tender after submission. Attempts to influence the procurement process may result in rejection of the tender. The procurement entity reserves the right to accept or reject any tender or annul the process entirely. 14. Successful tenderers must provide a bond guaranteeing satisfactory contract completion. Failure to meet contract obligations may result in forfeiture of the bond. 15. Tenderers who withdraw or fail to sign a contract after submission may be barred from future tenders for two years. 16. Successful tenderers are prohibited from using the award of a tender for advertising purposes. 17. Disputes arising from the tendering process will be resolved in the designated court. 18. The procurement entity reserves the right to examine and test products being procured. Suppliers must facilitate this process and replace any non-compliant products at their own expense. 19. They must indemnify the procurement entity against any claims of infringement. 20. Suppliers may not assign or transfer the contract without written consent from the procurement entity. 21. If a supplier becomes insolvent, the procurement entity may terminate the contract immediately. 22. For example, to detect non-compliance at a 10% frequency with 90% confidence, 22 samples per batch must be tested. 23. Chain-of-custody records must be maintained for all samples, including details of the source, condition, and transfer of samples. 24. Requests for pesticide sample analysis must be completed in duplicate and include all relevant details. These guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for the procurement, quality control, and management of public health pesticides, ensuring compliance with international standards and safeguarding public health.
